en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Brahmin Nyagrodha, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlaha,
Dharma Master and Imperial Preceptor of the Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, bestowed with the purple robe, and others, by imperial decree during the Western Heaven (India).
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Saṃgharakṣita. Having finished his midday meal on a certain day, he departed from Rājagṛha and went to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery to the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One, to behold, pay homage to, and attend upon him.
At that time, not long after the householder had departed, he thought to himself: "The early morning has already passed;
the Buddha and the bhikṣus are each in their own quarters. It would be appropriate to stop for now and not go to the Buddha's presence to pay respects and attend upon him."
"I shall now go to the place where the brahmin Nigrodha is gathered with his followers.

At that time, that brahmin was staying in the Udumbarikā Grove, surrounded by other brahmins, raising his voice and engaging in various discourses: namely, talk of kings, talk of war, talk of thieves, talk of clothing, talk of food, talk of women, talk of wine, talk of heterodox views, and miscellaneous talk, even extending to talk on the characteristics of the ocean and so forth.
"All such discourses are entirely bound to and attached to the worldly mind.
At that time, the brahmin Nyagrodha saw the householder Saṃyukta approaching from outside and immediately addressed the assembly, saying:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Cease!
You all should each lower your voices.
This person who has come is a śrāvaka disciple of the śramaṇa Gautama; he is a great householder residing in Rājagṛha, named Saṃgharakṣita."
This person is by nature reticent, and that which he has received and transmitted is likewise tranquil.
Therefore, you should speak in low voices; once he has become aware of this, he will then come here.
When the assembly of brahmins had heard these words, they all remained silent.
At that time, the householder Saṃghadatta came to the place where the brahmin Nyagrodha was, having arrived at that gathering.
Then, Nyagrodha rose to greet him, and they conversed with joy.
When their conversation was concluded, each sat to one side.
Then, the householder Saṃyukta addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying:
"In this assembly of yours, there is a distinction.

Just now I heard you raising your voices and engaging in various discourses—namely, discourses on kings, discourses on war, and so forth, even including discourses on the characteristics of the ocean. Such discourses as these are all attachments of the worldly mind, and are different from my World-Honored One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."

The World-Honored Buddha, within the wilderness, dwells, sits, and lies down according to his own pleasure; far removed from clamor and noise, cut off from the tracks of men, he maintains this state of tranquility.
"With the body staying in one place, the mind undistracted, focusing on a single object, act according to what is appropriate.
Then, the brahmin Nirgrantha said to the householder Saṃjaya:
"Householder!..."
"How shall I engage in debate with that ascetic Gautama?

If I initiate the discussion by posing a question based on a specific matter, his manifold wisdom will not be able to turn [the argument]. Since the ascetic Gautama dwells in an empty house, how could his wisdom possibly turn [against me]?"

Since wisdom could not function within the empty house, he then dwelt, sat, and lay down in a wilderness, far removed from clamor and cut off from human tracks. Maintaining this state in silence, his body remained in one place while his mind was undistracted; focusing single-mindedly on a single object, he acted in accordance with what was appropriate.
"Householder!
It is like a one-eyed ox wandering about the perimeter; you should know that how could such an ox possibly move?
The śramaṇa Gautama is just the same; dwelling in an empty house, how can his wisdom function?"
"Householder, if the śramaṇa Gautama should ever come to this assembly, I shall certainly engage him in debate.

I will establish the ultimate truth and initiate a line of questioning to strike at his position; I shall surely be victorious, while he will inevitably fall into defeat, like striking an empty jar, which is easily broken."

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in his own chamber, sitting in silent meditation; with his pure divine ear, he heard from afar the conversation between the householder Saṃyukta and the brahmin Nyagrodha as they were gathered together.
At that time, in the afternoon, the World-Honored One emerged from his own chamber.

At that moment, the rain had just cleared and the bright sunlight shone radiantly; he proceeded gradually toward the Anavatapta Lake (the Pool Without Poison), and having reached the shore of the lake, he walked slowly in meditation.
At that time, the brahmin Nigrodha saw from afar that the World-Honored One was on the bank of that pond; he immediately addressed the assembly, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is now here on the bank of the Sānuvīra Pond, walking slowly in meditation."
If he should come to this assembly, how would you receive him?
Would you rise to welcome him, engage him in conversation,
or simply leave your seats?
"Or perhaps he has vacated his own seat to summon me?
As he spoke these words, there spontaneously appeared one who came to arrange a seat for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and he further heard these words:
"Venerable Gautama, there is a seat here; you may take this seat as you please."
At that time, after the Blessed One had completed his alms-round on the bank of the pond of Goodness Free from Poison (Kalyāṇavāpī), he proceeded to where the brahmin Nyagrodha was staying.
Then, seeing the Blessed One approaching from afar, the brahmin addressed the assembly, saying:
"When the śramaṇa Gautama comes to this gathering, I shall pose a question to him."

And you, Gautama, within your system of law and discipline, by what practice of the Dharma can one who trains as a śrāvaka reach the state of peace, bring the inner mind to rest, and purify the brahmacarya?

At that time, when the World-Honored One arrived at that assembly, the multitude of brahmins spontaneously felt a surge of joy and delight; each rose from their seat and came forward to receive him with respect.
At that time, the brahmin Nyagrodha joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated himself, and said:
"Welcome, Gautama!"
"You possess universal knowledge; this is your seat, you should take your place.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Nyagrodha:
"You simply take your place on the seat prepared for me; as for myself, I know my own time, and I shall sit when I am ready."
At that time, the assembly of brahmins cried out in a loud voice:
"How rare! How extraordinary!
This śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Now, within this assembly, there is no one who has pointed it out; by means of my supernormal power, I know its location myself.
Then, the brahmin Nyagrodha engaged in pleasant conversation with the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and having finished that conversation, he withdrew and sat to one side.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying:
"The Tathāgata has now arrived at this assembly; what discourse or distinctions do you have?
The brahmin Nyagrodha replied to the Buddha:
"I have seen you coming from afar, and upon seeing you, I would immediately address the assembly, saying:
'When the śramaṇa Gautama comes to this gathering, I shall pose this question:
"Gautama, within your system of law and discipline, by what practice of the Dharma can one who trains as a śrāvaka reach the state of peace, bring the inner mind to rest, and purify the holy life?"'"
“Gautama! Since you have come here, I shall take this matter as the starting point for my inquiry; thus shall we engage in discussion and analysis with you.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the brahmin Nigrodha, saying:
“Nyagrodha! Regarding this matter, it is indeed difficult to know. Why is that?
"Different are the teachings, different are the views, different are the teachers, and different are the practices; you should instead pose your questions according to your own religious tradition.
At that time, the assembly of brahmins cried out in a loud voice:
"How rare! How extraordinary!"
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Regarding this matter you have asked, you do not answer by relying on your own teaching.
Instead, you are able to provoke a line of inquiry within the teachings of others, and then respond according to those questions."
Then, the brahmin Nigrodha said to the Buddha:
"If my methods, views, teachers, and practices are different from yours, it will be difficult for me to understand your Dharma and Discipline."

I now inquire of you regarding our own Dharma teaching: how should one practice so as to attain liberation and purity, to attain supreme whiteness, to attain reality, and to dwell within that pure reality?
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying:
“I shall now briefly explain the practice cultivated within your system, O Nyagrodha.

You claim that one can attain the fulfillment of the four precepts, that one can practice them, and that one can attain the most supreme excellence; yet through such prior cultivation of renunciation, you do not diminish your various desires.”
"Niṣadha! What are the four precepts that you uphold through your practice? They are:

not killing oneself, not commanding others to kill, and not rejoicing in killing; not stealing oneself, not commanding others to steal, and not rejoicing in stealing; not speaking falsehoods oneself, not commanding others to speak falsehoods, and not rejoicing in speaking falsehoods; and not engaging in sexual misconduct oneself, not commanding others to engage in sexual misconduct, and not rejoicing in sexual misconduct."
"You, Nigrodha!
By means of such things as these, you claim that you have attained the fourfold perfection of the precepts. Nigrodha!"
How is it that you are able to practice?
As for your practice, you claim that dwelling and sitting in high places, or standing on tiptoe, constitutes the practice of the Dharma;
or that constantly consuming bitter, astringent, coarse, and foul food constitutes the practice of the Dharma.
Some practice the Dharma while dwelling in quiet, empty spaces;
some practice the Dharma without shaving their hair and beards;
some practice the Dharma by lying down upon thorns, or by sleeping on woven rafters.
Some dwell constantly in lofty, cloud-reaching heights as their practice of the Dharma;
others remain bound to a single location as their practice of the Dharma, even bathing their bodies three times a day.
"Thus, through various kinds of pressing afflictions and sufferings, you treat the body and practice the Dharma.
Such matters as these constitute your method of practice, O Nyagrodha."
"What, Nigrodha, do you consider to be the renunciation for which you, the ascetic,
practice? Nigrodha,
as for the practice of renunciation you cultivate, it is the belief that one attains renunciation by exposing the body."
Furthermore, when the matter of eating and drinking is finished, one should lick the hands to ensure purity.
One should not accept food or drink offered by those with frowning faces or those with angry countenances;
nor should one eat in the middle of streets or alleys.
He does not abide among swords, staves, or weapons.

He wanders through cities and towns in silence, remaining mute; he does not speak of where he has come from, nor of where he is going, nor of where he dwells; he utters neither words of opposition nor compliance, nor does he utter various kinds of speech, nor does he offer any discourse whatsoever.
Or one may accept food from a single household;
or accept food from two, three, or even up to seven households;
or accept food from only one household and not from any other household.
Some do not eat for one day;
some for two, three, or even up to seven days; or again, they do not eat for half a month or a full month.

Regarding food, they do not eat parched grain, nor rice, nor beans, fish, or meat; nor do they consume cow’s milk, clarified butter, curd, oil, or honey. They drink no wine, no sweet syrups, and no fermented vinegar, but subsist on nothing but water strained from chaff and husks to sustain their lives.

Furthermore, they constantly eat vegetables, or eat weeds such as *tīra* and *priyaṅgu*, or eat *gomaya* (cow dung), or eat medicinal shoots and medicinal roots, or eat dried raw rice and grains, or eat various other coarse and bitter herbs and greens;

or they wear but a single garment, or wear garments of grass, or garments of *kuśa* grass, or garments of tree bark, or garments made of firewood, or garments made of the bark of fruit trees, or garments made of disheveled hair from the charnel grounds, or garments of sheep’s wool, deer hair, or deer skins, or garments of the wings of the *tṛṇaja* bird, or garments of the wings of the owl.
“Nigrodha, such practices as these are what you, the practitioner Nigrodha, reckon to be the path of renunciation.
Nigrodha, do these practices truly lead to renunciation and purity?”
Have you attained the most supreme purity?
Have you attained reality?
Have you attained dwelling within the purity of reality?
Then, the brahmin Nigrodha said to the Buddha, “So it is,
so it is, Śramaṇa Gautama!”
This practice of mine results in liberation and purity, attains the most supreme whiteness, and achieves reality; it brings about dwelling within the purity of reality.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Nyagrodha: “Nyagrodha!

These practices you cultivate and such matters as these do not lead to renunciation; they do not lead to the purity of renunciation; they do not attain the highest whiteness; they do not attain reality; they do not attain dwelling in the purity of reality; rather, within the dharma of practice, you have attained but a small portion.”
The brahmin Nyagrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Although what you have said is indeed most excellent."
"However, this practice of mine results in the attainment of supreme liberation, the attainment of reality, and the attainment of the unsurpassed.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Nyagrodha:

"Furthermore, as for your own practice, you claim that you can attain the fourfold perfection of the precepts, that you can practice them, and that you have attained the most excellent and superior state."
Having previously practiced renunciation, one does not diminish the various desires.
While observing the four precepts, one dwells together with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
First, one arouses loving-kindness toward the eastern direction, contemplating it as complete in its practice, vast and universal, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from harm.

Thereafter, in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—in all worlds—one is endowed with a mind of loving-kindness; the fulfillment of one's practice is likewise thus.
"Niṣṭhā! Do you think that by practicing in this way, you can achieve liberation and purity?
Can you achieve the highest, most immaculate state?"
"Have you attained the truth?
Do you abide in the purity of the truth?
At that time, the brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is, Śramaṇa Gautama!
This practice of mine has indeed attained liberation and purity, attained supreme whiteness, and attained reality; it dwells within the purity of reality."
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying: "Nyagrodha!

These practices that you cultivate are not for the sake of renunciation and purity; they do not attain the most supreme whiteness; they do not attain reality; nor do they abide in the purity of true reality."
"You claim there is something to be attained; this, too, is not true.
The brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying, "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
What you have said is indeed excellent;
however, my practice leads to liberation, it leads to purity, it leads to reality, and it leads to the unsurpassed.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Nyagrodha: "Nyagrodha!
Furthermore, regarding your practice, you claim: 'I am able to attain the fourfold perfection of precepts; I am able to practice; I have attained the most supreme excellence.'"
While practicing renunciation as before, he does not diminish his various desires;

that is to say, by means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), he is able to know the events of one, two, or three births, up to a hundred births in the past.
"Niṣṭhā! Do you think that by practicing in this way, you can attain liberation and purity?
Can you attain the supreme whiteness?"
"Have you attained the truth?
Do you abide in the purity of the truth?
At that time, the brahmin Niṅguda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is, Śramaṇa Gautama!
This practice of mine has indeed attained liberation and purity, attained supreme whiteness, and attained reality; it dwells within the purity of reality."
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying: "Nyagrodha!
These practices of yours, such as these, do not lead to deliverance or purity; they do not attain the highest whiteness; they do not attain reality; nor do they abide in the purity of true reality."
"Although there is something attained, it is not real.
The Brahmin Nyagrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!"
What you have said is indeed excellent;
however, this practice of mine leads to liberation and purity, it leads to reality, and it leads to the unsurpassed.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying: "Nyagrodha!
Furthermore, regarding your practice, you claim: 'I am able to attain the perfection of the four precepts; I am able to practice; I have attained the most supreme excellence.'"

Having previously practiced renunciation, yet without diminishing his various desires, he is able to perceive all sentient beings in the world with his pure divine eye—whether they are being born or passing away, whether beautiful or ugly, whether reborn in fortunate realms or unfortunate realms, whether noble or base—seeing them all according to their karmic retributions.
"Niṣṭhāya! Do you think that by practicing in this way, you can attain liberation and purity?
Can you attain supreme stainlessness?"
"Have you attained the truth?
Do you abide in the purity of the truth?
At that time, the brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So it is, so it is, Śramaṇa Gautama!
This practice of mine has indeed attained liberation and purity; it has attained the highest whiteness, as well as reality, and dwells within the purity of reality."
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying: "Nyagrodha!
Although such matters as these, practiced by you, are indeed pure, that which I teach is this: even with such practice as yours, one has not yet escaped the proliferation of various afflictions."
The brahmin Nyagrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
How is it that although my practice is pure, you, Gautama, say that I have not yet abandoned the various afflictions that increase in accordance with them?"
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nigrodha, saying: "Nigrodha!

You practitioners cultivate yourselves for the sake of manifesting the merits of your practice, thinking: 'Because I have cultivated and perfected such practices, those kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and brāhmaṇas will surely respect, revere, and make offerings to me.'"
"Niṣṭhā! This is precisely that which you practice wherein the afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"

Although you practice, you rely on what you have cultivated and give rise to an attitude of arrogance, looking down upon and despising others; this is precisely how afflictions increase in accordance with your practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
As you practice, you give rise to the mind of self-conceit and overweening pride; this is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions in your practice."
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
In your practice, you disparage and insult other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, saying:

"You śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas sustain your lives with various kinds of food; you consume all five kinds of seeds in the world, namely: root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, superior-seeds, and seed-of-seeds. It is by these five kinds that you maintain your lives."
"O Nyagrodha!
Thus you wander about, uttering words of contempt and insult, seeking out disputes with such swiftness and sharpness as the flash of lightning; you crush and destroy others like frost and hail."
"Niṣṭhāya! This is precisely that which you practice, wherein afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhāya!"

While you are practicing the path, you may see other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are respected, honored, and provided for by their own peers and the like; upon seeing this, you give rise to various feelings of resentment and jealousy, and say:
"These śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas subsist on their lives by greedily consuming many kinds of food, yet they are instead respected, honored, and provided for by others."
"I have always sustained my life with nothing but bitter, astringent, empty, and insipid things.
For what reason do these other people not show me respect and offer me sustenance, as they do for the Nyagrodha?"
"This is precisely that which increases your afflictions through the practice you are cultivating.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Brahmin Nyagrodha, Volume Upper.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on the Brahmin Nyagrodha, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlagupta,
Dharma Master and Imperially Conferred Purple Robe, Subject and Monk, together with others,
under imperial decree during the Xia Tian Dynasty: "Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"
While you are practicing, if you only pose questions in the presence of the Tathāgata or his disciples, resentment will immediately arise.
Once anger and vexation have emerged, obstacles will be created; because of these obstacles, various faults will arise.
"Nigrodha!
This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions through your practice.
Furthermore, Nigrodha!"
As you practice, if you inquire about the True Dharma from the Tathāgata or from a disciple of the Tathāgata, at that time the Buddha, the Tathāgata,
will with a single-minded focus skillfully explain it for you, providing a definitive teaching as appropriate to dispel all your doubts.

Yet you all rely on external treatises to offer your explanations, contradicting one another in your desire to subvert the true principle; instead, you claim that my question is an improper discrimination.
"Niṣṭhā! This is precisely that which you practice, wherein afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"

In your practice, you recognize that the Buddha Tathāgata, or the disciples of the Tathāgata, truly possess supreme and preeminent virtues worthy of reverence; yet, despite this, you fail to show them such reverence.
"Niṣṭhā! This is precisely that which you practice wherein afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"
There are practitioners who feel revulsion toward beneficial matters,
yet do not give rise to revulsion toward harmful matters.
Among these two types of matters, if you do not give rise to revulsion toward harmful matters, [you are at fault].
"Nigrodha! This is precisely that which you practice, wherein afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Nigrodha!"
In your practice, you give rise to the mark of conceit and manifest it by thinking, "I am able to practice.
Niṣṭhā! This very thing is the increase of afflictions within your practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhāya!
In your practice, you may obtain rare and exquisite food and drink, yet you become attached to their flavors and give rise to discrimination, saying:
'This is what I enjoy; this is what I do not enjoy.'"
"If it is what you desire, I shall accept it.
Through this grasping, he gives rise to attachment; because of that attachment, he conceals his faults. Therefore, despite possessing superior wisdom, he fails to achieve liberation.
Regarding the remaining food and drink, if you do not take pleasure in them yet still cling to them with greed and attachment,
and only relinquish them with great reluctance—
Nigrodha, this is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions in your practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
When you practitioners dwell in secluded places, sitting in silence with the marks of a virtuous person, if someone comes and asks:
'In what dharma are you proficient? "
"Furthermore, regarding what dharma do you not understand? Yet you,
sirs, claim 'I do not understand' concerning that which you have understood,
and claim 'I understand' concerning that which you do not understand."
In these many ways, all such instances are called "false speech arising from correct awareness. Niṣṭhā!
This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions within your own practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
In your practice, you constantly give rise to anger and resentment. Niṣṭhā!"
This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions within your practice.
Furthermore, Niṅguda!
In all your practices, you are without shame and without remorse in every respect.
“Nigrodha! This is precisely that which you practice wherein the afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Nigrodha!”
In your practice, you constantly give rise to indolence and inferior diligence.
Niṣṭhā! This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions within your practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
In your practice, you are constantly lacking mindfulness and lack clear comprehension. Niṣṭhā!"
"This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions within your practice.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhāgata!
In your practice, your minds are distracted and your faculties are diminished."
Nigrodha! This is precisely that which you practice wherein the afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Nigrodha!

In your practice, you give rise to harmful intent and remain fixed in your former state of mind; you do not seek liberation, but look only toward yourselves, truly giving rise to grasping and attachment toward these phenomena.
"Niṣṭhā! This is precisely that which you practice wherein the afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"
In your practice, your wrong views are deep-seated and you perform perverted dharmas.
Niṣṭhā! This is precisely what causes the afflictions to increase further through your practice.
"Furthermore, Nyagrodha!
In your practice, you reckon that which is without limit to be finite; your arising of views is likewise so.
Nyagrodha!"
This is precisely what constitutes the increase of afflictions within your practice.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
In your practice, you constantly give rise to thoughts of craving and aversion.
"Niṣṭhāyin!
This is precisely that which increases your afflictions through practice.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhāyin!"
In your practice, you are ignorant, dull-witted, and obscured regarding all that is to be practiced.
Niṣṭhā! This is precisely how the afflictions increase in accordance with your practice.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!
In your practice, you are unable to listen or receive instruction, being like those who are deaf; you have nothing to teach or demonstrate, resembling sheep that are mute."
"Niṣṭhāya! This is precisely that which you practice wherein the afflictions increase.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhāya!"

In your practice, you take pleasure in committing sinful deeds and likewise delight in associating with those who commit such deeds; thus, you are bound by and brought under the control of evil friends.
"Niṣṭhā! This is precisely that which increases your afflictions through practice.
Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"

In your practice, you have given rise to overweening pride, conceiving the notion that you have attained what you have not; you claim to see what you have not seen, to have done what you have not done, to have attained what you have not attained, to know what you do not know, and to have realized what you have not realized.
Nigrodha! This is precisely that which you practice, wherein the afflictions increase. Nigrodha!
What do you think?
Regarding the various afflictive phenomena described above, is there any class of practitioners who possesses these qualities?
The Brahmin Nyagrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Is it only this one class of practitioners who possesses such afflictions?"
"In my opinion, their number is very great.
The Buddha said to the brahmin Niṅtuó:
"As I have stated above, your practice is intended to manifest the merits and achievements of your cultivation."
Because I have cultivated and perfected such practices, I cause those kings, ministers, kṣatriyas, and brahmins to respect, revere, and make offerings to me.

Nigrodha! If you were to act in such a manner merely to display the fruits of your spiritual practice, so that kings, ministers, and others might offer you respect and offerings, even to the point of giving rise to overweening pride;

They harbor the conceit of attainment: they claim to have seen what they have not seen, claim to have done what they have not done, claim to know what they do not know, claim to have attained what they have not attained, and claim to have realized what they have not realized.
All such things as these are impure; they are all entirely accompanied by the increase of afflictions. You should know that they are all subsumed within the defiled portion. Nigrodha!
What do you think?
Regarding what I have said above— such matters as these and such practices— does one thereby attain liberation and purity,
or does one attain supreme, stainless whiteness?
“Have you attained the truth?
Do you abide in the purity of the truth?
The brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying:

"So it is, so it is, Śramaṇa Gautama! For those such as ourselves, practicing in this way, this leads to deliverance and purity; this attains the most supreme whiteness; this attains the truth; this attains dwelling within the purity of truth."
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying:
"I shall now speak to you according to reality.
Regarding what you have just asked me:"
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
Within your system of law and discipline, by practicing what dharma can one who trains as a śrāvaka reach the state of peace, bring rest to the internal mind, and purify the holy life?”
"What you have thus asked is indeed true.
You should know that the place of cessation for the śrāvakas is the most supreme among the superior, being exceedingly lofty and excellent; it is the dwelling place of cessation for all noble ones."
At that time, the assembly of brahmins all praised him together, saying:
"How marvelous! How marvelous!"
“Śramaṇa Gautama!
Within his system of law and discipline, all that is done is refreshing.

At that time, having heard these words, the householder Saṃyukta realized that the assembly of brahmins present had conceived a slight degree of longing for the Buddha, the World-Honored One. He then addressed the brahmin Nyagrodha, saying:
“Nyagrodha! Regarding what you have just said,
as you engaged in mutual debate with the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and established the ultimate truth—
having raised a single point of inquiry to strike at him— I should have emerged victorious while he would surely have fallen into defeat, like striking an empty jar, which is easily broken.”
"Why do you not now pose a question?
The Buddha said to the brahmin Niṅguda:
"What do you think?"
“Did you truly utter such words?
The brahmin Nigrodha addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Śramaṇa Gautama!”
"I have indeed spoken such words.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Niṅguda, saying: "Niṅguda!"

Have you not heard what the ancient masters, the former virtuous ones, the elders, the veterans, and the wise have said: that even the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, like yourselves, now gather in assembly and raise their voices to engage in various discourses—namely, discourses on kings, discourses on war, discourses on thieves, discourses on clothing, discourses on food, discourses on women, discourses on wine, discourses on heterodox views, and discourses on manifold trivialities—and so on, even including discourses on the characteristics of the ocean and such?

"Niṣṭhā! Or perhaps you have heard what the ancient masters have said: that the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, just as I am now, dwell, sit, and lie down in the wilderness, far removed from clamor and noise, cut off from the tracks of men, and maintaining this state of solitude."
“With the body staying in one place, the mind undistracted, and focused on a single object, does one act as is appropriate?
The brahmin Nigrodha replied to the Buddha,
“It is so, Gautama!”

I have also heard what was said by the ancient masters, the former worthies, the elders, the veterans, and the wise: that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, are not like us who, at this present time, gather together and raise our voices to utter various discourses.

That is to say, discourses on kings, discourses on war, discourses on thieves, discourses on clothing, discourses on food, discourses on women, discourses on wine, discourses on heterodox views, and discourses on manifold trivialities, and so forth, even including discourses on the characteristics of the ocean and other such things.

I have also heard what the ancient masters have said: that the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, just as you are now, dwell, sit, and lie in the wilderness, far removed from clamor and bustle, cut off from the tracks of men, maintaining this state of solitude.
"Abiding with the body in one place, the mind undistracted, focusing on a single object, one should act as is appropriate.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin Nigrodha, saying: "Nigrodha!"
When you heard the ancient masters speak in the past, did you not reflect thus:
"Those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to teach the Dharma according to what is appropriate; having awakened to it themselves, they further teach the Dharma of awakening to others;
having attained liberation themselves, they further teach the Dharma of liberation to others."
"Having attained peace for myself, I further teach the Dharma of peace to others.
Having attained nirvāṇa for myself, I further teach the Dharma of nirvāṇa to others.
Thus spoke the Buddha, O Nyagrodha!
At that time, you returned and said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus, making distinctions regarding the duties and activities of the Teacher's Dharma."
Furthermore, it was said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama makes such a statement as that there is conceptual differentiation regarding the practice of dwelling in tranquility.
Moreover, it was further said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus: 'In that teaching of the teacher Nigaṇṭha, there is a collection of sinful and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, he says:
'The śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus: "In that teaching of the teacher Nigaṇṭha, many kinds of wholesome dharmas have become dispersed. "
Furthermore, it is said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama speaks thus because he wishes to proclaim those causal conditions.
One should not view these various kinds of statements in such a way.
"Nigrodha! Why should one not hold such a view?
It is because the teachings of those various teachers, their respective practices, and even all their causal conditions and matters are entirely different."
"Niṅgūḍha!

For this reason, I do not speak of the teacher’s activities regarding the Dharma, nor do I speak of his activities regarding dwelling in tranquility; nor do I say that within that teacher’s Dharma there is a gathering of sinful and unwholesome states, nor do I say that within that teacher’s Dharma there is a dispersal of various wholesome states, nor do I wish to speak of the causal conditions thereof."
“Nyagrodha! I always say this:

‘If there is a true person who is not sycophantic, not crooked, and not deceitful—a practitioner of right conduct—I shall teach and instruct him with the Dharma, guiding him according to what is appropriate.’”

May that noble being, in accordance with my correct exposition and correct instruction, for seven years, or perhaps six, five, four, three, two, or one year, remain single-mindedly undistracted, free from all feverish afflictions, purifying body and mind, and applying themselves with focused intent.
"I say that such a person sees the Dharma and knows the Dharma; they transcend the first two fruits and proceed directly to the third fruit, the stage of *anāgāmin* with remainder.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā! [The Buddha continued:]
I have always said this:

"If there is a true person who is without flattery or crookedness, and who is not deceitful or false, but practices correctly, I shall for that person's sake preach the Dharma and provide instruction, guiding them according to what is appropriate."

May that noble person, in accordance with my correct teaching and instruction, for a period of seven months, or six, five, four, three, two, one month, or even half a month, remain consistently undistracted, free from all feverish afflictions, with body and mind purified, and single-mindedly intent upon their pursuit.
"I say that such a person sees the Dharma and knows the Dharma; they transcend the first two fruits and proceed directly to the third fruit, the stage of the Anāgāmin with remainder.
"Furthermore, Niṣṭhā!"
I have always said this:

"If there is a true person who is without flattery or crookedness, and who is not deceitful or false, and who practices correctly, I shall then preach the Dharma for them, instruct them, and guide them as is appropriate."

May that noble person, according to my correct explanation and correct instruction, for seven days, or perhaps six, five, four, three, two, one, half a day, or even from before a meal until after a meal, remain consistently undistracted, free from all feverish afflictions, with body and mind purified, and single-mindedly intent on seeking [the goal].
"I say that such a person sees the Dharma and knows the Dharma; they transcend the first two fruits and proceed directly to the third fruit, the stage of *anāgāmin* with remainder.

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken these words, all the members of the assembly of brahmins—whose obstructions and karmic burdens were deep and heavy—had no realization; their bodies and minds were confused and disordered, sinking into a state of stupor and delusion.
Those various eloquences were unable to be deployed; they lowered their heads in silence and remained there, dwelling in anxious thought.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this matter, looked toward the householder Saṃgharakṣita and said:
"Householder!
These people are truly deluded.
Having obscured both seeing and hearing, they further sever all speech, like someone using an object to stuff their own mouth.
Their defilements are thus profound; this is a great demonic deed.
They were unable to pose this question to the Buddha, the Tathāgata:
"O Śramaṇa, within your Dharma and Vinaya, by what practice of the Dharma can those who train as śrāvakas reach the state of peace, bring their inner minds to rest, and purify their brahmacarya?"

At that time, the World-Honored One, having taught, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened the householder Saṃgharakṣita by preaching the Dharma according to his needs, emitted from his body a light that was vast, blazing, and all-pervasively illuminating.
Thereupon, in the midst of the assembly, he leaped into the air and returned to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery.
[The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Brahmin Nyagrodha, Volume II]
